# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, name the folders the change touched** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Leave out test folders, README edits, and above all any file whose diff is comments only.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- bump-version: Raise the project's version — a minor bump by default. Use when the owner says "bump version".
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that just landed can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use at the end of every change, beside the conversation capture — not on request.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-migration-plans: How to order the phases of an implementation or migration plan so nothing stalls mid-run — front-load the out-of-band setup, collapse the review gates into one stacked-PR pass, leave only executable steps — and how to keep its tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use when writing or reviewing a migration plan or a phased implementation plan, and when working through one's tracking issue.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.mjs or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.

Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.

Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. - simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

// THE ENGINE VERSION — the single number that says which engine release a repo is
// running (docs/versioned-updates/DESIGN.md §2). The engine root vendors wholesale,
// so this module ships into every mount with the rest of the engine, and a member's
// stamp records the value it received (vendoring/apply-vendor-set.mjs). That pair is
// what makes "installed version → target version" answerable on the member side:
// which engine migrations still apply, and whether a pack's minimum is satisfied.
//
// A MONOTONIC INTEGER, not semver. Every comparison the update flows make is
// "installed < target" over a totally ordered sequence — migrations are ranged
// vN→vN+1 — so an integer is the whole requirement, and a three-field string would
// buy a parser plus two components nothing reads.
//
// ADVANCED BY RELEASE, never by an ordinary change: a release is a snapshot that has
// passed the live canary rehearsal once (DESIGN §2.1), and the bump is what declares
// that happened. An engine migration is written against the version it lands in — it
// applies to repos below that number.
export const ENGINE_VERSION = 6;
===
# Versioned updates — design

Status: **agreed** (owner decisions recorded in §10; settled in the
2026-08-12 design conversation). Supersedes, once migrated, the unified
**baselining** task (`packs/basics/tasks/baselining/`) — its nightly
converge-everything-at-canon-head model, its date-held stamp, and its
four-condition agent escalation. The phased rollout is tracked as a
migration-plan issue (linked from the PR that lands this doc).

Terminology decision (owner): the mechanism is called **update** — engine
update, pack update, install. The words *baseline / baselining /
rebaselining / rebasing* retire with the task that carried them.

The shape: the canon splits into a **versioned engine** and **versioned
packs**, each with its own update flow. The engine update is fully
deterministic — no agentic stage, ever. The pack update keeps a bounded
agentic stage ("apply the new pack rules to this repo; repair what they
break") with one terminal escape hatch: any non-green end state leaves the
PR open, tagged `need-human`. Installing a pack is the same runner as
updating one, started from version zero.

---

## 1. Why the current mechanism has an agentic stage at all

The census (2026-08-12, this repo's full history — no migration record has
ever been deleted, so the population is complete): **three agentic notes
ever written**, across eleven migration records, plus three structural
escalation conditions in `worker.mjs`'s `escalation()`:

| Residual | Cause | Lands in |
|---|---|---|
| `pack-independence` note | engine composition contract | member local packs |
| `prework-rename` note | engine field rename | member local packs |
| `fleet-baseline-task` note | pack lever conversion | member `.github/workflows/` |
| `withheld-workflows` | credential (Action token cannot write `.github/workflows/`) | — |
| `selftest-failed` / `checks-not-green` | judgment: is a non-green converge safe to merge? | — |
| executor-routine verification | the CCR routine is invisible to Actions | — |

The lesson that shapes this design: the residuals split by **type**
(credential / judgment / member-content adaptation), not by which half of
the corpus changed. Two of the three notes were engine-caused but landed in
member-authored local packs the canon has never seen. So the split below
does not *eliminate* those types — it **relocates each to the one flow that
can absorb it**, and constrains the engine so its flow needs none of them.

## 2. The engine: versioned, cloned, never agentic

1. **The engine has running versions.** A release is a qualified snapshot
   (the live canary rehearsal runs against it once, per release, instead of
   the fleet discovering breakage per repo per night).
2. **The update procedure clones the engine release into the repo's mount**
   — wholesale replacement, as `compute-vendor-set` does today. The engine's
   own files never need migration; they are replaced.
3. **Engine migrations cover the member-owned files that reference engine
   surfaces** (hooks in `.claude/settings.json`, paths in local-pack code,
   the declaration file). They are **usually regex-replace rules, rarely
   code — never agentic** (owner decision). **The vendoring flow fetches
   only the migrations above the repo's installed engine version** (owner
   decision) — the version replaces today's date-based recency window
   (`recordDirIsRecent`) as the fetch predicate: an up-to-date repo
   vendors none, a lagging repo vendors exactly its gap. Because the same
   window currently also drives `migrationActive()` — the legacy-tolerance
   predicate consumer checks consult — that tolerance becomes
   version-based in the same move ("tolerate the legacy shape while
   installed version < N"), or checks would flag legacy shapes on repos
   that simply have not updated yet. The discipline this imposes on
   engine evolution is accepted and explicit: an engine contract change must
   either be mechanically expressible (regex or a small deterministic
   codemod shipped with the release) or remain backward-compatible, with the
   legacy shape accepted and normalized at load — the posture
   `prework-rename` already took. A contract change that satisfies neither
   **does not ship** until it does. There is no agentic lane to fall back
   on, by construction.
4. **The engine update does not write `.github/workflows/`.** The rare
   engine change that must touch a workflow file ships as a **custom
   update** — an explicitly named, separately credentialed operation (the
   Action token structurally cannot write there; the custom update runs
   under an MCP-credentialed session or a human). Naming it keeps the lane
   from becoming an invisible agentic side door.
5. **The engine update merges its PR to main automatically**, gated on the
   converged tree passing `selftest --strict` — the gate that exists because
   of #555, where an engine change silently stopped every consumer pack from
   validating while content checks stayed green. On a red self-test the PR
   stays open, tagged `need-human`. A **`force-merge-on-red-ci`** option
   (owner decision) overrides the gate for the operator who has judged the
   red acceptable — an explicit per-invocation flag, never a stored default.

## 3. Packs: versioned, deterministic core, bounded agentic tail

6. **Each pack has a version number**, and **each pack version declares the
   minimum engine version it requires**, enforced by the updater: a pack
   update never applies past the installed engine (§5). This is what makes
   the split coherent — the current single-snapshot guarantee ("the set and
   the content can never come from different snapshots") is replaced by a
   *checkable* compatibility constraint rather than dropped.
7. **A pack update is deterministic first**: vendor the new pack version,
   run its version-ranged migrations (vN→vN+1, in order), converge wiring.
   **Pack migrations live in the pack's own `migrations/` folder** and are
   fetched by the same version gate as the engine's (owner decision): only
   the records above the repo's installed version of *that pack* ship in
   the mount. The flat canon-wide `migrations/` directory does not survive
   the split — each record moves to the flow (engine or pack) that owns it.
   **Workflow churn belongs to the pack flow, explicitly** (owner decision):
   the scheduler workflow's content is a function of the *task set*
   (`declaredSecrets` unions `required_secrets` across discovered tasks), so
   pack changes are what rewrite it, and the pack flow carries the
   credential to land those files — the MCP lane baselining's agent stage
   uses today, §2b of its task.
8. **A pack update may carry an agentic stage**: "apply the new pack rules —
   fix the repo, repair the tests." This is the one place agentic work
   survives, because it is the one residual no mechanism can absorb: the
   pack's new rules meet member-authored content the canon has never seen.
   The stage also inherits the orphaned **executor-routine verification**
   (the CCR routine that fires on `ready-for-agent` is not a GitHub
   artifact; only an agent session can see it, and this is the only agent
   lane left).

   **The word is *may*, and the RECORDS are what decide it** (#798). A pack
   record declares `applyStage: { why, instructions }`; an update whose gap

content.content:
# Engine releases

The engine ships as a **version**, not a stream of commits: `ENGINE_VERSION` in
[`version.mjs`](version.mjs) is what a member's stamp records, what an engine
migration's range is written against, and what a pack's `minEngineVersion` is
checked against (`docs/versioned-updates/DESIGN.md` §2). This file is the log of
those versions and the evidence behind each.

## What a release is

**A release is the commit that bumps `ENGINE_VERSION`, and a bump is only
legitimate once the live canary rehearsal has passed against the tree being
released** (owner decision, 2026-08-12). There is no tag and no separate release
artifact: the updater clones `main` at its newest bumped ref, so the version lives
in the file the mount already carries and there is nothing to cut, push or forget.

The canary is what makes the snapshot *qualified*. It converges a real adopting
repo — running **its own** vendored worker, the copy a member would run — against
the ref under test, and asks whether that repo still works. The fixture rehearsal
on every PR only tests what someone remembered to model; this is the other half.

## Releasing

1. Have the change ready on its branch, CI green.
2. Dispatch **Canary rehearsal** with `ref` = your branch
   (`.github/workflows/canary-rehearsal.yml` → Run workflow), and wait for it.
   A red canary is not a release — fix the branch and rehearse again.
3. In the same change: bump `ENGINE_VERSION`, and add a row below for the new
   version linking the run that passed.
4. Merge. The version now on `main` is the release.

`engine-release-record` (the canon's own local pack) refuses a bump that arrives
without its row, or with a row citing no run — the canary runs in another
repository, so its run id is the only durable evidence the release was rehearsed,
and every member in the fleet is stamped with the number it qualified.

A change that touches the engine **without** bumping the version is an ordinary
engine edit and needs none of this; members receive it on their next converge as
they always have. The bump is what says "this snapshot has been qualified" — so
bump when a migration needs a version to range against, or when a release is
worth naming, not on every merge.

## The log

| Version | Date | Canary rehearsal | What it released |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2026-08-12 | [run 31628529342](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/31628529342) | The first numbered engine: version scaffolding, the versioned stamp, and migration records re-homed under their owning flow (#769). |
| 2 | 2026-08-12 | [run 31633584458](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/31633584458) | Migration records gain regex rewrites and the `normalizeLocalDeclarations` codemod, and `local-pack-namespace` starts rewriting local-pack declarations to `local/<id>` — the first release whose records actually change a member's own files. |
| 3 | 2026-08-13 | [run 31655440833](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/31655440833) | Baselining retired (#768 Phase 5): the task, its escalation codes and the `migrations/` compatibility entry points are gone, the `agentic:` migration field is rejected rather than ignored, and `updates` becomes the default mechanism. Freshness is measured by version rather than by the age of a ref the update flows never write. |
| 4 | 2026-08-14 | [run 31826589868](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/31826589868) | A `needs-human` dispatch issue no longer stops its task (#821): the scheduler's guard suppresses on a live claim rather than on any open issue, so an escalation awaits triage instead of shutting the lane until a person closes it by hand. Bounded — a second unresolved escalation holds the lane, under a verdict of its own that leads the run summary. |
| 5 | 2026-08-19 | [run 32267881121](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/32267881121) | The pack renames (#1022): `core` → `claudinite-lifecycle`, `grow_with_claudinite` → `claudinite-growth`, and the scheduled-task authoring contract moved between them. The record converges each member's declaration and moves its mount directories; the loader tolerance (`engine/pack_loader/renamed-packs.mjs`) makes that record's timing irrelevant by resolving both spellings, so no member can be caught holding a declaration and a mount that disagree — which for the pack carrying `update` would cost it the machinery that delivers its own repair. |
| 6 | 2026-08-19 | [run 32270294377](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/32270294377) | The declaration half of the pack renames (#1041). Version 5 moved every member's mount directories and stamped `packVersions` keys but never rewrote the `packs` array: it did that textually, anchored on `"packs": [` so a member's own `{ "from": "core" }` barrier rule could not be caught by accident, and the anchor could not cross the nested array in an entry object like `{ "id": "barriers", "via": ["basics"] }`. Replaced by a structural op (`applyPackRenames`) driven by the engine's own rename map. A separate record because a repo already stamped 5 never runs the 5 record again — and a converged member is exactly the one whose declaration still needs moving. |

Version 1's rehearsal is the automatic post-merge run against `8dbb096`, the
commit that introduced the constant — the procedure above landed after it, so
there was no branch to rehearse first. Version 2's was dispatched against its
own branch at `6607b7c`, which is this change's tree; the only edit after it is
the row you are reading.

Version 3's was dispatched against `9f5162a` — this change's tree, with only the
row you are reading edited after it — and it is the first rehearsal in weeks that
actually rehearsed anything. The gate had been driving the canary's
vendored BASELINING worker, which stood down and exited 0 the moment the canary
flipped to `updates` — a green step that converged nothing, for every core
change since 2026-08-12. Version 2's rehearsal predates the flip and was real;
what run 31654827686 qualifies is both this tree and the repaired gate, which
now fails unless the run says in words that it converged.

Version 4's was dispatched against `e416aed1` — this change's tree, with only the
run id in the row you are reading edited after it.

Version 5's was dispatched against `93ca7bd` — this change's tree, with only the
run id in the row you are reading edited after it. It converged the canary through
BOTH flows (`update: engine`, then `update: packs`) and the converged tree passed
its self-test, which is what qualifies the rename specifically: the canary held a
declaration and a mount spelled the old way when the run began, and the packs
loaded anyway.

input.title: Engine and pack versions become date-anchored: `<ymmdd>.<n>`
input.body:
Engine and pack versions are monotonic integers today (`ENGINE_VERSION = 6`, `version: 13`). A number says nothing about *when* a version was cut, so "is this member behind, and by how long?" needs a second lookup every time.

Move both to a date-anchored form, `<ymmdd>.<n>` — `(year - 2020)*10000 + month*100 + day`, then a running number within that day. The first version cut on 2026-08-20 is `60820.1`, the second `60820.2`.

Ordering is unchanged in meaning: compare the day part, then the running number. Every legacy integer sorts below every date-anchored version (`6 < 60820.1`), so a member stamped under the old scheme reads as behind, which is what it is.

**Scope** — every site that creates, stamps, compares or scrapes a version:

- `engine/version.mjs` (`ENGINE_VERSION`), every `packs/*/pack.mjs` `version:`
- the comparators in `updates/{engine-update,pack-update,install}.mjs`
- `engine/checks/helpers/active-migrations.mjs` (record `version:` scrape, `migrationApplies`)
- `engine/pack_loader/pack-schema.mjs` (`isVersion`)
- the text scrapers in `packs/claudinite-dashboard/fleet.mjs` and `packs/claudinite-fleet-sheepdog/tasks/fleet-roster/drift-issues.mjs`
- the canon's own local checks `pack-version-bumped` and `engine-release-record`

**Migration technique**: every reader accepts both forms for one week; the legacy tolerance is removed in its own change once the fleet has re-stamped.

1	// THE ENGINE VERSION — the value that says which engine release a repo is running
2	// (docs/versioned-updates/DESIGN.md §2). The engine root vendors wholesale, so this
3	// module ships into every mount with the rest of the engine, and a member's stamp
4	// records the value it received (vendoring/apply-vendor-set.mjs). That pair is what
5	// makes "installed version → target version" answerable on the member side: which
6	// engine migrations still apply, and whether a pack's minimum is satisfied.
7	//
8	// DATE-ANCHORED, `<day>.<n>` — the shape, the ordering and why the corpus versions
9	// this way rather than in semver are stated below the constant. Every comparison made
10	// of this value is "installed < target" over a total order, so the format buys one
11	// thing over the plain counter it replaced: the version says when it was cut, without
12	// a second lookup.
13	//
14	// ADVANCED BY RELEASE, never by an ordinary change: a release is a snapshot that has
15	// passed the live canary rehearsal once (DESIGN §2.1), and the bump is what declares
16	// that happened. An engine migration is written against the version it lands in — it
17	// applies to repos below that value.
18	export const ENGINE_VERSION = '60820.1';
19	
20	// THE VERSION FORMAT — how every engine and pack version in the corpus is written,
21	// read and ordered. The helpers below are imported by every side that creates a
22	// version (each `packs/*/pack.mjs`), stamps one (updates/), compares two (the update
23	// planners, the dashboard, the fleet roster) or scrapes one out of source text over
24	// the API. They live beside the constant rather than in a module of their own so the
25	// engine surface a member's mount must carry for any of it is one file.
26	//
27	// THE SHAPE IS `<day>.<n>` — `60820.1`, displayed with a leading `v`. The day part
28	// is `(year - 2020) * 10000 + month * 100 + day`, so 2026-08-20 is 60820; the second
29	// part is the running number of versions cut on that day, starting at 1. It is a
30	// STRING and never a float: `60820.10` and `60820.1` are different versions and the
31	// same number.
32	//
33	// Anchoring the year on 2020 rather than taking its last digit is what keeps the day
34	// part monotonic past 2029 — 2030 reads 100101, above every 2029 value, where a
35	// last-digit year would wrap to 0 and sort a decade of releases underneath.
36	//
37	// WHY DATE-ANCHORED AT ALL. Every comparison the update flows make is still
38	// "installed < target" over a total order — nothing here needs semver's three
39	// components. What the plain counter could not do is say WHEN: a member stamped at 6
40	// against a canon at 13 is behind by an unknown amount of time, and the fleet
41	// surfaces that as a number a reader has to go and date by hand.
42	//
43	// LEGACY TOLERANCE, until 2026-08-27 (#1101). Versions were plain positive integers
44	// until 2026-08-20, and the integers are still sitting in every member's stamp, in
45	// each pack's `minEngineVersion` floor and in every migration record's range. So a
46	// legacy integer parses here as `<n>.0` — below every date-anchored version, which
47	// is exactly where a member that has not re-stamped belongs. Pure dependency-free,
48	// like the manifest spec it serves.
49	
50	// The day part of a Date, in UTC. Callers that have a `YYYY-MM-DD` string already
51	// (the corpus passes `today` around in that form) can hand it straight over.
52	export function versionDay(when = new Date()) {
53	  const d = typeof when === 'string' ? new Date(`${when.slice(0, 10)}T00:00:00Z`) : when;
54	  if (Number.isNaN(d.getTime())) return null;
55	  return (d.getUTCFullYear() - 2020) * 10000 + (d.getUTCMonth() + 1) * 100 + d.getUTCDate();
56	}
57	
58	// A date-anchored version, as its two parts. The day part is at least five digits
59	// (2020-01-01 is 101, but nothing predates the scheme, and the smallest day a repo
60	// can carry is 60820), which is what keeps it unambiguously apart from a legacy
61	// counter — those never reached three figures.
62	const DATE_ANCHORED = /^([1-9]\d{4,5})\.([1-9]\d*)$/;
63	
64	// A version in EITHER form, as `{ day, seq }`, or null when the value is not one.
65	// A legacy integer is `{ day: n, seq: 0 }` — the same tuple shape, so every
66	// comparison below is written once and knows nothing about the two spellings.
67	export function parseVersion(v) {
68	  if (typeof v === 'number') return Number.isInteger(v) && v > 0 ? { day: v, seq: 0 } : null;
69	  if (typeof v !== 'string') return null;
70	  const m = DATE_ANCHORED.exec(v.trim());
71	  return m ? { day: Number(m[1]), seq: Number(m[2]) } : null;
72	}
73	
74	export const isVersion = (v) => parseVersion(v) !== null;
75	
76	// True for the retiring spelling only — the one thing the removal change (#1101)
77	// greps for, and what a reader needing to say "this predates the scheme" asks.
78	export const isLegacyVersion = (v) => typeof v === 'number' && Number.isInteger(v) && v > 0;
79	
80	// Order two versions: negative when `a` is older. An UNPARSEABLE version is not an
81	// error and not a zero — it sorts as equal to everything, so a caller that cannot
82	// price one side reports "no gap" rather than inventing one in either direction.
83	// Callers that must distinguish absence from equality check `isVersion` first.
84	export function compareVersions(a, b) {
85	  const x = parseVersion(a);
86	  const y = parseVersion(b);
87	  if (!x || !y) return 0;
88	  return x.day - y.day || x.seq - y.seq;
89	}
90	
91	export const versionAbove = (a, b) => compareVersions(a, b) > 0;
92	
93	export const formatVersion = ({ day, seq }) => `${day}.${seq}`;
94	
95	// The next version to cut today, given the one that stands. A new day restarts the
96	// running number at 1; a second version on the same day is `.2`. A `current` that is
97	// legacy, absent or unparseable simply does not constrain today's number — the day
98	// part is already above every integer the old scheme ever reached.
99	export function nextVersion(current, today = new Date()) {
100	  const day = versionDay(today);
101	  const held = parseVersion(current);
102	  return held && held.day === day ? `${day}.${held.seq + 1}` : `${day}.1`;
103	}
104	
105	// The version-shaped fragment for the text scrapers — the readers that lift a
106	// version out of `engine/version.mjs` or a `pack.mjs` fetched over the API, where
107	// there is nothing to import. Kept here so the six of them cannot disagree about
108	// what a version looks like; each wraps it in its own anchor.
109	export const VERSION_SOURCE = String.raw`\d+(?:\.\d+)?`;
110	
111	// What such a scraper should hand back: the literal as it was written, so a legacy
112	// integer stays a number and a date-anchored version stays a string, and every
113	// comparison downstream is the same one function.
114	export function versionFromLiteral(text) {
115	  if (text == null) return null;
116	  const t = String(text).trim();
117	  const v = t.includes('.') ? t : Number(t);
118	  return isVersion(v) ? v : null;
119	}

The lesson that shapes this design: the residuals split by **type**
(credential / judgment / member-content adaptation), not by which half of
the corpus changed. Two of the three notes were engine-caused but landed in
member-authored local packs the canon has never seen. So the split below
does not *eliminate* those types — it **relocates each to the one flow that
can absorb it**, and constrains the engine so its flow needs none of them.

## 2. The engine: versioned, cloned, never agentic

1. **The engine has running versions.** A release is a qualified snapshot
   (the live canary rehearsal runs against it once, per release, instead of
   the fleet discovering breakage per repo per night).
2. **The update procedure clones the engine release into the repo's mount**
   — wholesale replacement, as `compute-vendor-set` does today. The engine's
   own files never need migration; they are replaced.
3. **Engine migrations cover the member-owned files that reference engine
   surfaces** (hooks in `.claude/settings.json`, paths in local-pack code,
   the declaration file). They are **usually regex-replace rules, rarely
   code — never agentic** (owner decision). **The vendoring flow fetches
   only the migrations above the repo's installed engine version** (owner
   decision) — the version replaces today's date-based recency window
...
   (owner decision) overrides the gate for the operator who has judged the
   red acceptable — an explicit per-invocation flag, never a stored default.

## 3. Packs: versioned, deterministic core, bounded agentic tail

6. **Each pack has a version number**, and **each pack version declares the
   minimum engine version it requires**, enforced by the updater: a pack
   update never applies past the installed engine (§5). This is what makes
   the split coherent — the current single-snapshot guarantee ("the set and
   the content can never come from different snapshots") is replaced by a
   *checkable* compatibility constraint rather than dropped.

# /do-later — defer a change into a chained request run

The owner has spotted a change that should happen **after** the work in front of
them. Doing it now derails the session; an ordinary issue waits for somebody to
remember it. This files it as an **ad-hoc request** (tasks-dispatch DESIGN §16):
an issue the queue picks up on its own, held behind what is still in flight.

You are filing work, not doing it. Touch no source file, open no branch.

## What you write

**One issue, well defined.** The run that implements it will never see this
conversation — the issue body is the whole brief. State the change, the files or
surfaces it touches if you know them, what "done" looks like, and anything the
owner ruled out. Size it to its idea; a rename is a sentence.

Give the body these two lines, verbatim in this spelling — the tick reads the
first one:

```
Blocked-by: #<what this waits on>

<!-- filed by /do-later -->
```

**What it waits on**, first match wins:

1. the issue of the **previous `/do-later` you filed in this session** — that is
   the chain the owner asked for, each deferral behind the last;
2. otherwise the **pull request** the session's work is on, if one is open;
3. otherwise the **issue** the session is working on;
4. otherwise nothing — omit the field, and say in your reply that it queues
   immediately.

Only ever name blockers that will actually *close* — a merged PR does, a branch
does not. If you filed an earlier `/do-later` this session but no longer have its
number, find it by its marker line among the repo's open issues rather than
falling back to (2).

## The labels — the mark, the model, the merge

Apply all three (`mcp__github__issue_write`, `labels`):

- **`claude-task`** — the mark. The next tick adopts the issue into a work item,
  blocked on what you named, and releases it once those close.
- **`claude-model:<family>`** — the family **this** session is running, so the
  deferred work is done by what the owner is working with now. Read it with
  `get_session` (claude-code-remote, `session_id` omitted) and map
  `session_context.model` to `opus`, `sonnet` or `haiku`. A model outside those
  three has no label — omit it and the run takes the default.
- **`claude-automerge`** — the standing authorization to land the change without
  the owner's approval **when the run's diff turns out to be narrow** (docs,
  tests, comment-only edits, and code within a single directory; the run measures
  this, not you). **Withhold it whenever the owner said they want to see this
  one** — "let me review it", "show me before merging", or any such wording
  outranks how small the change looks.

If a label does not exist in the repository yet, the mark cannot be applied (the
API refuses an unknown label, and only the tick creates them). Say so in your
reply and leave the issue filed — the labels appear on the next tick, and the
owner can mark it from the issue page.

## Then say what you filed

One line back to the owner: the issue link, what it waits on, the model family,
and whether it will merge itself or come back for approval.

input.head: claude/version-format-migration-1mb5vp
input.title: Engine and pack versions become date-anchored `<day>.<n>`
input.body:
Closes #1100.

Versions were a plain monotonic counter. It orders releases, which is all the update flows need, but it says nothing about *when* one was cut: a member stamped at `6` against a canon at `13` is behind by an unknown amount of time, and every fleet surface reporting that gap makes a reader go and date it by hand.

Both the engine and every pack now version as `<day>.<n>` — `60820.1`, where the day part is `(year - 2020) * 10000 + month * 100 + day` and the second part is the running number of versions cut that day. Displayed with a leading `v`, as the surfaces already do.

Two decisions worth naming:

- **The year is anchored on 2020, not taken as its last digit.** A last-digit year wraps to `0` in 2030 and sorts a decade of releases underneath every 2029 one. `2026 → 6` either way, so the example holds and the ordering survives.
- **A version is a string.** `60820.10` and `60820.1` are different versions and the same float, so nothing in the corpus may parse one as a number.

### The migration technique

Every reader accepts **both** spellings. A legacy integer parses as `<n>.0`, which sorts below every date-anchored version — exactly where a member that has not re-stamped belongs, so no fleet surface has to special-case it. The tolerance is scheduled for removal in its own change, #1101, once the fleet has converged; the parser's own comment carries that date and issue number.

Legacy integers deliberately stay in two places for now: each pack's `minEngineVersion` floor and every migration record's `version:` range, both of which are references to engine versions that really were plain counters. #1101 retires them.

### What changed, by folder

- **`engine/`** — `version.mjs` gains the format: `parseVersion`, `compareVersions`, `versionsEqual`, `nextVersion`, `versionDay`, and `VERSION_SOURCE`, the regex fragment the text scrapers share so the six of them cannot disagree about what a version looks like. The helpers live beside the constant rather than in a module of their own, so the engine surface a mount must carry for any of it is one file. `ENGINE_VERSION` becomes `'60820.1'`. `pack_loader/pack-schema.mjs` validates both spellings, and `checks/helpers/active-migrations.mjs` reads a record's range and ranges over it through the shared comparator.
- **`updates/`** — the three planners (`engine-update`, `pack-update`, `install`) compare through `versionAbove` instead of `>` and gate on `isVersion` instead of `typeof === 'number'`.
- **`packs/`** — all 33 manifests move to `'60820.1'`. The dashboard's `fleet.mjs` and the sheepdog's `fleet-roster/drift-issues.mjs` scrape and compare through the shared helpers.
- **`.claudinite/local/packs/`** — `pack-version-bumped` and `engine-release-record`, the two canon-side checks that read a version out of a diff, do the same; the first now names `nextVersion(base)` as the remedy rather than `base + 1`.
- **`vendoring/rehearsal/fixtures.mjs`** — the `versioned-local` shape gains a second local pack carrying the date-anchored spelling. This is the `consumer-safe-change` answer: the manifest vocabulary widened, additively, and the fixture is what proves a consumer-authored manifest still validates in **both** spellings.

`ENGINE_VERSION` moving is an engine release, so it lands with its `RELEASES.md` row citing the canary rehearsal dispatched against this branch.

input.title: Remove the legacy single-integer version tolerance
input.body:
#1100 moved engine and pack versions to date-anchored `<day>.<n>` and left every reader accepting a legacy positive integer as well, parsed as `<n>.0`. That tolerance was scoped to one week — **from 2026-08-27** — by which point every member converging nightly has re-stamped under the new format. This issue removes it.

**Do not start before 2026-08-27.** Before removing anything, confirm no member still stamps a legacy integer: the fleet roster's mount probe already reads each member's `claudinite.engineVersion` and `packVersions`. If any member does, comment with which ones and re-defer rather than breaking their converge — a stamp the parser rejects reads as "no version installed", which re-applies every migration record in the corpus.

**What to remove**

- `engine/version.mjs` — the number branch of `parseVersion`, `isLegacyVersion`, the `LEGACY TOLERANCE` paragraph, and the `'?` optional-quote groups in the scraper anchors that exist only to read an unquoted integer. `VERSION_SOURCE` tightens to the date-anchored shape.
- The legacy integers still standing in the canon, which are what the tolerance is carrying by then:
  - each pack's `minEngineVersion` floor (`packs/*/pack.mjs`) — a floor at `1` constrains nothing and should go rather than be converted; `claudinite-dashboard` (`4`) and `claudinite-canary-repo` (`3`) are real floors below the oldest engine any live member runs, so they go the same way.
  - every migration record's `version:` range (`engine/migrations/*/`, `packs/*/migrations/*/`). A record whose range predates the format applies to nobody by then; check `migrationApplies` against each member's stamp before deleting one.
- The `PACK_VERSIONED` fixture's legacy spelling in `vendoring/rehearsal/fixtures.mjs`, and the zero/legacy assertions in `engine-tests/version.test.mjs`.

Keep `parseVersion`'s treatment of **zero** — that is the install floor (`docs/versioned-updates/DESIGN.md` §3), not a legacy version.

**Done** when `grep -n "isLegacyVersion\|legacy" engine/version.mjs` is empty, no `version:` or `minEngineVersion:` in the tree is a bare integer, and the full suite plus `check_the_world` are green.

Blocked-by: #1105

---
name: writing-migration-plans
description: How to order the phases of an implementation or migration plan so nothing stalls mid-run — front-load the out-of-band setup, collapse the review gates into one stacked-PR pass, leave only executable steps — and how to keep its tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use when writing or reviewing a migration plan or a phased implementation plan, and when working through one's tracking issue.
---

# Writing migration and implementation plans

A plan's phases are not a narrative of the work; they are a **schedule of who has to be present
when**. Ordering them by topic — "phase 1: the store, phase 2: the workers, phase 3: cutover" —
scatters the moments that need a human across the whole run, and every one of them stops it. Order
them by *what blocks*, and the run ends with a stretch nobody has to attend.

Everything below assumes the change is already agreed: the problem, and that this migration is the
right way to solve it (basics' *Starting any requested change*). The end-state's **shape** —
converging in one forced pass, accepting legacy input at the door, a standing mechanism for
stragglers — is [RULES.md](../../RULES.md)' *Planning a migration*; this skill is the ordering.

## The three blocks, and where each belongs

Sort every step of the plan into one of three kinds, and let that sort — not the subject matter —
decide the phase it lands in.

**1. Out-of-band setup — before any code changes.** Anything performed outside the repo that a
later step will need: provisioning an environment, creating a session or runner, setting a secret
or variable, granting a permission, flipping a platform setting, registering a webhook. Nearly all
of it is **non-destructive** — it adds a capability that nothing yet consumes, so doing it early
costs nothing and changes no behaviour. Doing it *late* costs the whole run: the plan reaches the
step that reads the secret and stops until someone is available.

Front-load all of it into phase zero, before the first line of code. Write it as its own issue
with a checkbox per step (basics' *Handing over a human-only step*), stating for each what stays
broken while it is off. And before writing it down, confirm you genuinely cannot do it yourself —
a step handed to a human that you could have taken is the most expensive kind of block there is.

The exception is the genuinely destructive step — deleting the old store, revoking the old
credential, removing the compatibility shim. Those are not setup; they are the migration's tail,
and they belong after the cutover has been observed working.

**2. Review and authorization gates — collapsed into one pass.** Every phase that ships code is a
gate: the owner must read it and approve it before the next phase can start. A plan with four
coding phases has four such waits, and each one is dead time whose length nobody controls.

Write **all** the code first, as a stack of PRs each based on the previous, and put the whole
stack in front of the owner together. The stack keeps the reviewable units small and independent —
one concern per PR, as ever — while costing one arrival of attention rather than four. Merge it
base-first once approved.

Approval of the stack is approval of the stack: it does not extend to a fix authored afterwards
(basics' *Acting on an approval to merge, ship or proceed*).

**3. Execution steps — whatever is left.** Once phase zero has landed the setup and the stack has
merged, the remaining steps run the migration: force the converge, backfill the members, watch the
cutover, retire the shim. If the first two sorts were done properly there is no gate among them —
they can be run at will, in one sitting, by whoever is at the keyboard.

That is the test of the plan. **Read the phases in order and mark every point where the run would
have to stop and wait for a person.** Each mark that falls after phase zero and the review pass is
a step that was sorted wrong. Move it, or say in the plan why it genuinely cannot move.

## Writing it down

- **The plan is a tracking issue**, and the phases are its checkboxes. Status and remaining work
  live there; a design document, where the project keeps one, carries the mechanism and not the
  progress.
- **Each phase names its exit condition**, observable and stated as a thing that reads back true —
  not "cutover done" but "every member's stamp shows the new ref". A phase whose end is a judgment
  call is a phase that stays open.
- **Nothing closes on a human's memory.** A step you cannot verify now gets a mechanism that comes
  to you — a scheduled task, a watched PR, an issue something converges (basics' *When verifying now
  is genuinely impossible*). A phase whose closing condition is "check next week" is not a phase.
- **Size each step to what it is**, and don't restate in the plan what the design document or the
  linked issue already carries.

## Working through the plan

Once the plan is agreed, the issue body's plan is **append-only**. While implementing, tick its
checkboxes and add below it — a comment, or a new section for what the work turned up — and never
edit, reword, condense or re-order what was already there.

The body is the record of what was agreed, and it is the only copy: an edit overwrites it in place
with nothing left to diff against, so a plan silently rewritten to match what was built reads
afterwards as a plan that was followed. Keeping it fixed is what makes the divergence visible —
and a divergence is the interesting part, not an embarrassment to tidy away.

So when the work shows a phase was wrong, say so **underneath**: what the plan assumed, what turned
out to be true, and what you did instead. If that changes the plan going forward, the new steps are
an addition, appended and dated; the superseded ones stay where they are, marked superseded rather
than deleted.

The exception is a **correction to the plan itself before implementation of it starts** — the owner
saying the plan misreads what they asked for. That is a correction (basics' *Acting on a
correction*): repair the body, since there is no work yet for it to have diverged from.

## Reviewing someone else's plan

Run the same sort over it. The findings worth raising, in order of what they cost:

1. A secret, permission, environment or account created **after** code that depends on it.
2. More than one review gate — two or more phases that each end in "open a PR and wait".
3. A destructive step scheduled before the replacement has been observed working.
4. A phase with no stated exit condition, or one only a person can judge.
5. A step handed to a human that the agent could have performed itself.

p='packs/basics/skills/writing-migration-plans/SKILL.md'
s=open(p).read()

credential, removing the compatibility shim. Those are not setup; they are the migration's tail,
and they belong after the cutover has been observed working."""
new = """The exception is the genuinely destructive step — deleting the old store, revoking the old
credential, removing the compatibility shim. Those are not setup; they are the migration's tail,
and they belong after the cutover has been observed working. **The tail is not a phase**; see the
compatibility window below for what carries it instead."""
assert old in s; s=s.replace(old,new)

old = """## Writing it down"""
new = """## The compatibility window, and why it is not a phase

A migration that changes a *representation* — a version format, a field's shape, a wire word, a
file layout — has a shortcut past most of the sort above, and it is worth reaching for
deliberately. Land it as **one change in which every reader takes both spellings and every writer
produces only the new one.** The old data keeps working where it stands, the new data is correct
from the first commit, and there is no cutover to schedule because there is no moment when
something must be true of everything at once.

remember is there. Do **not** write it into the plan as a later phase. A "remove the shim" phase is

run that would have done it ended weeks earlier, and nothing brings it back. File it instead as
work that comes back on its own (basics' *Spotting a change that should wait*), in the **same
change that opens the window**, and write into it:

- **The date or condition the window closes on**, and the observable that settles it — not "once
  everyone has migrated" but "no member's stamp still holds the old form", read from the thing that
  already reads it.
- **The full removal list.** The run that does it will not have this conversation: name every
  reader that took both, and every place the old spelling still legitimately stands.
- **What must survive the removal.** A tolerance usually sits next to something that looks
  identical and is not — a real zero beside an absent value, a legacy spelling beside a reserved
  one — and the removal run needs telling which is which.

that stops and which issue removes it. The comment and the queued issue are one fact in two places,
and the one a future reader hits first is the code.

The same shape answers finding 3 below. A destructive step you can defer into a dual-read window
does not need to be scheduled against the cutover at all — it needs the window, and the issue that
closes it.

## Writing it down"""

open(p,'w').write(s)

input.body:
Stacked on #1105 — it edits `packs/basics/`, whose version #1105 already moves, so this one bases on that branch and bumps to `60820.2`. Merge #1105 first; this retargets to `main` on its own.

The technique #1105 used is worth writing down, and the skill that should carry it is the one about ordering a plan's phases. A representation migration — a version format, a field's shape, a wire word, a file layout — can skip most of the sort the skill describes: land one change in which every reader takes both spellings and every writer produces only the new one, and there is no cutover to schedule, because there is no moment when something must be true of everything at once.

What that leaves is the tolerance, and this is the part worth a rule. A plan that writes "remove the shim" as a later phase has written the archetype of the phase that never closes — it has no owner at the moment it becomes due, and the run that would have done it ended weeks earlier. The section says to file that tail as work that comes back on its own, **in the same change that opens the window**, and names the three things the issue has to carry: the observable that closes it, the full removal list, and what must survive the removal (a tolerance usually sits next to something that looks identical and is not — a real zero beside an absent value). The expiry is also carried at the site, since a future reader hits the code before the issue.

The permission list for FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN was spelled in six sweeps'
"token is not set" messages, each the subset its own author needed, plus
a seventh in RULES.md that was the only complete one. Nothing in the
machinery held it — required_secrets carries a name — so those strings
were the only machine-readable statement of the requirement, and a
session assembling an adopting repo's handover from them landed the
union of the subsets it happened to read.

That is how missingbulb/Shepherd adopted one permission short. Pull
requests read is the row only the digest needs, and a fine-grained PAT
reads a public repo's pull requests without it, so four sweeps ran green
for two days while the digest died on the fleet's first private member
as a bare 403 — and, because the failed work item stayed open, the task
stopped being scheduled rather than merely failing.

fleet-token.mjs now holds one row per permission with the sweep that
forces it. Every sweep takes its token from requireFleetToken(), which
throws the whole grant; the pack declares adoptionHandover, rendered
from the same rows, so the install flow prints the complete list at the
one moment somebody is present to grant it; RULES.md and the task docs
point there instead of restating a subset.

The new tests fail against the previous tree on both counts: the pack
declared no handover, and the roster sweep spelled its own list.

The rename split the two spellings by FILE TYPE — .md got the prose word, every
other file got the field word — so prose living inside .mjs comments and inside
JSON string values came out wearing the field's underscore. The owner caught it
on a waiver reason in .claudinite-checks.json.

The rule is about the token, not the file: code_work is the declaration field
(beside agent_model, expected_outcome) and keeps the underscore wherever it names
that field, backticked, quoted, followed by a colon, or as .code_work; everything
else reads code-work. Applied to comment lines, two JSON prose strings, and the
strings a human actually reads — a triage issue's "code-work exited 1" and the
work item's delivered-artifacts heading.

That heading is also MATCHED, not just written: withSection locates the section
it already wrote so a re-entrant run updates it in place. Renaming it alone would
have appended a second section to every in-flight item carrying the old one, so
the heading is now a shared constant with its two earlier spellings beside it,
and withSection takes aliases to find a section under any of them. Proven by
removing the alias lookup and watching the new test report two sections.

Owner review on #827: the file that holds only declarations should not be
code. A pack's declarations are now the array in
packs//declared-checks.json (a skill's in its own beside checks.mjs),
discovered structurally by the pack registry and compiled by the pattern
engine — no import, no manifest line; writing the declaration adds the check.

The format drops what the declaration was borrowing from prose. No comments

no `description` and no `doc` pointer — a declaration states its own case —
and `why` is renamed `failureMessage` for what it is: the line the agent
reads when the check fires. Regexes are strings in /pattern/flags form,
compiled at load; a path-or-pattern key still reads a plain string as an
exact path, and a plain string anywhere else is reported with the key that
got it.

The registry reaches the compiler lazily, only where a declaration file
exists, so a tree carrying just the pack machinery loads as before. Both
deliberate cross-tree reaches are accepted with reasons.

Findings are unchanged: the world sweep is finding-for-finding identical to
main, and `--list` matches on id and severity for all 88 rules (a declared
rule now prints its failureMessage where a coded rule prints its
description, and no doc pointer). 1613 tests pass, six of them new — the
regex-string compilation, the authoring-error message, failureMessage on the
finding, the loader's cache, and the registry discovering a pack's and a
skill's declarations — each seen to fail against a mutated engine.

D2 and C3 of #768, together because they are the same change.

THE RENAME. The mechanism and the task that runs it were one letter apart —
`mechanism: "updates"` and `FORCE_TASKS=update` — and they appear together, in
the same declaration and the same dispatch UI. `versioned` is what the design has
called this scheme all along ("versioned updates"); `update` stays the task's
name, which is right for a thing a repo DOES.

It travels as a pack record rather than a converge because the mechanism is a
DECLARATION — the repo's own statement, in the file that also holds its pack
list, interview answers and every reviewed `accept`. Nothing in the update flows
rewrites that file wholesale, deliberately. So: one version-ranged record, a
literal rewrite, idempotent after it drains.

THE FIRST RECORD TO DECLARE `applyStage` (#798), and a real one rather than a
demonstration. The rewrite is exhaustive over the declaration; what it cannot
reach is a member's OWN prose about how it is maintained — a README, a local
pack's rules, a workflow comment. The canon has never seen those, which is
precisely the boundary the apply stage exists on.

AND THE FIRST `basics` BUMP, 1 → 2, which is what makes the record reachable at
all: `migrationApplies` is `want > have` against the stamped version, and what
gets stamped is the manifest's number. The manifest now states that invariant
where the next person will bump it.

BOTH NAMES ARE LIVE while the record drains. A member reads its own declaration
with the engine it currently has, one cycle behind the record that renames it —
so if the old spelling stopped parsing on landing, a correctly-declared repo
would read as `invalid` for exactly one cycle and be reported as misdeclared.
The worker's guard moved from `mechanism !== 'updates'` to `servedByUpdates()`
for the same reason: it is vendored, and a literal there would refuse a member
the moment its declaration was correctly renamed. The vocabulary loses `updates`
a release later, once no member carries it.

Driven against a real member tree: pass one rewrites the declaration and asks for
the stage naming the record; pass two applies nothing and asks for nothing.

Two gaps left open by #791 and #802, both of the same shape: a silence that
reads like health.

pendingSchedulerWorkflow swallowed every failure to a bare `null` — the same
answer it returns for "already converged". A member whose settings stopped
parsing would report a clean update forever while its wiring silently froze,
which is precisely the failure #797 exists to end. It still does not throw (this
is one surface of an update whose other surfaces have landed, and a member with
an unrelated fault must not be stranded behind it), but it now returns
{ pending, error } and the error rides out on `detail` — the line the worker
already prints, which becomes the PR body and the dispatch issue's reason.
Chosen over a new field because a new field only reaches a member once its
worker catches up a cycle later; `detail` reaches every fielded worker today.

And the applyStageBrief shim carried its removal condition in a comment, which
is a comment nobody rereads — a shim kept forever is indistinguishable from one
still needed. It now has a failing-test expiry at engine 5, with instructions to
check a real member's vendored worker rather than just bump the number.

{"total_count":49,"workflow_runs":[{"id":32371716136,"name":"CI","display_title":"CI","workflow_id":317526095,"run_number":1068,"run_attempt":1,"event":"workflow_dispatch","status":"in_progress","head_branch":"claude/migration-plans-dual-read-window","head_sha":"a5d4347ee3aa830f4ea9b1ec14ab7b0c1a3076ac","head_commit":{"message":"writing-migration-plans: the compatibility window, and why it is not a phase

A representation migration — a version format, a field's shape, a wire word —
has a shortcut past the phase sort: land one change in which every reader takes
both spellings and every writer produces only the new one. There is then no
cutover to schedule, because there is no moment when something must be true of
everything at once.

What it leaves is the tolerance, and a plan that writes "remove the shim" as a
later phase has written the archetype of the phase that never closes: nothing
brings it back at the moment it becomes due. The skill now says to file that
tail as work that comes back on its own, in the same change that opens the
window, and names what the issue has to carry — the observable that closes it,

The permission list for FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN was spelled in six sweeps'
"token is not set" messages, each the subset its own author needed, plus
a seventh in RULES.md that was the only complete one. Nothing in the
machinery held it — required_secrets carries a name — so those strings
were the only machine-readable statement of the requirement, and a
session assembling an adopting repo's handover from them landed the
union of the subsets it happened to read.

That is how missingbulb/Shepherd adopted one permission short. Pull
requests read is the row only the digest needs, and a fine-grained PAT
reads a public repo's pull requests without it, so four sweeps ran green
for two days while the digest died on the fleet's first private member
as a bare 403 — and, because the failed work item stayed open, the task
stopped being scheduled rather than merely failing.

fleet-token.mjs now holds one row per permission with the sweep that
forces it. Every sweep takes its token from requireFleetToken(), which
throws the whole grant; the pack declares adoptionHandover, rendered
from the same rows, so the install flow prints the complete list at the
one moment somebody is present to grant it; RULES.md and the task docs
point there instead of restating a subset.

The new tests fail against the previous tree on both counts: the pack
declared no handover, and the roster sweep spelled its own list.

The rename split the two spellings by FILE TYPE — .md got the prose word, every
other file got the field word — so prose living inside .mjs comments and inside
JSON string values came out wearing the field's underscore. The owner caught it
on a waiver reason in .claudinite-checks.json.

The rule is about the token, not the file: code_work is the declaration field
(beside agent_model, expected_outcome) and keeps the underscore wherever it names
that field, backticked, quoted, followed by a colon, or as .code_work; everything
else reads code-work. Applied to comment lines, two JSON prose strings, and the
strings a human actually reads — a triage issue's "code-work exited 1" and the
work item's delivered-artifacts heading.

That heading is also MATCHED, not just written: withSection locates the section
it already wrote so a re-entrant run updates it in place. Renaming it alone would
have appended a second section to every in-flight item carrying the old one, so
the heading is now a shared constant with its two earlier spellings beside it,
and withSection takes aliases to find a section under any of them. Proven by
removing the alias lookup and watching the new test report two sections.

input.body:
Engine and pack versions are monotonic integers today (`ENGINE_VERSION = 6`, `version: 13`). A number says nothing about *when* a version was cut, so "is this member behind, and by how long?" needs a second lookup every time.

Move both to a date-anchored form, `<ymmdd>.<n>` — `(year - 2020)*10000 + month*100 + day`, then a running number within that day. The first version cut on 2026-08-20 is `60820.1`, the second `60820.2`.

Ordering is unchanged in meaning: compare the day part, then the running number. Every legacy integer sorts below every date-anchored version (`6 < 60820.1`), so a member stamped under the old scheme reads as behind, which is what it is.

**Scope** — every site that creates, stamps, compares or scrapes a version:

- `engine/version.mjs` (`ENGINE_VERSION`), every `packs/*/pack.mjs` `version:`
- the comparators in `updates/{engine-update,pack-update,install}.mjs`
- `engine/checks/helpers/active-migrations.mjs` (record `version:` scrape, `migrationApplies`)
- `engine/pack_loader/pack-schema.mjs` (`isVersion`)
- the text scrapers in `packs/claudinite-dashboard/fleet.mjs` and `packs/claudinite-fleet-sheepdog/tasks/fleet-roster/drift-issues.mjs`
- the canon's own local checks `pack-version-bumped` and `engine-release-record`

**Migration technique**: every reader accepts both forms for one week; the legacy tolerance is removed in its own change once the fleet has re-stamped.

---

**Status**

- #1105 implements it. Engine release `60820.1`, qualified by canary rehearsal [run 32371130795](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/32371130795) against `1f05d43`.
- #1106 is the queued removal of the legacy tolerance, blocked behind #1105, not to start before 2026-08-27.
- #1107 (stacked on #1105) writes the technique into the `writing-migration-plans` skill.

Two things the implementation settled that the brief did not:

- The year is anchored on **2020**, not taken as its last digit — `2026 → 6` either way, but a last-digit year wraps in 2030 and sorts a decade of releases underneath.
- A version is a **string**. `60820.10` and `60820.1` are different versions and the same float.

Legacy integers deliberately stay in two places until #1106: each pack's `minEngineVersion` floor and every migration record's `version:` range, both of which are references to engine versions that really were plain counters.

- uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
          # Check out the PR's real head, not the synthetic refs/pull/N/merge commit
          # actions/checkout uses by default — otherwise HEAD is an ephemeral merge of
          # the branch into main, which the work-scoped squash-merge-history check would
          # (correctly, for that synthetic commit) flag. This makes CI evaluate exactly
          # what the local Stop hook does: the branch tip. Falls back to github.sha on push.
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.sha }}
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
      - name: Unit tests
        # THE test roots — a closed set of FOLDERS, each swept to any depth. Depth is
        # deliberately not enumerated: the previous form spelled out one glob per level of
        # nesting, so a test at an unlisted depth was silently never run — which is exactly
        # how vendoring/'s two files sat outside CI. `**` removes depth from the question;
        # what remains is the root list, and engine-tests/ci-test-roots.test.mjs fails the
        # moment a tracked test lands outside it. Adding a root is a deliberate CI edit;
        # adding a test is not.
        #   engine-tests/            engine/ (migrations included) + the other top-level canon code;
        #                            mirrors engine/'s inner structure, and stays canon-side
        #                            because engine/ ships to consumers exactly as-is (#385)
        #   packs/                   every canon pack's tests, each inside the pack it covers
        #   vendoring/               co-located with the vendor computer/writer they cover,
        #                            the fixture-consumer rehearsal included
        #   dev/tools/               maintainer-side tooling nothing at session time runs
        #   .claudinite/local/packs/ this repo's own local packs — tests live inside the tree
        #   docs/tasks-dispatch/sim/ the dispatch design's executable scenarios — the
        #                            simulator lives beside the spec it models, not in
        #                            engine/ (nothing ships it; it tests prose)
        # nullglob: a root with no tests drops out instead of reaching node as a literal pattern.
        run: |
          shopt -s globstar nullglob
          tests=(engine-tests/**/*.test.mjs packs/**/*.test.mjs vendoring/**/*.test.mjs dev/tools/**/*.test.mjs .claudinite/local/packs/**/*.test.mjs docs/tasks-dispatch/sim/**/*.test.mjs)
          # Deliberately oversubscribed. node --test defaults to one worker per core
          # minus one, which fits a CPU-bound suite; this one spends most of its wall
          # clock waiting — on git plumbing, spawned workers and converge fixtures — so
          # the cores idle at that default (measured on this tree: 106s wall against
          # 187s of user+sys on 4 cores). Doubling the workers: 106s -> 70s, with 16
          # buying only another 2s.
          node --test --test-concurrency=$(( $(nproc) * 2 )) "${tests[@]}"
      - name: Conformance sweep (world scope)
        # The tree as it stands — the pattern bootstrap wires into consumers.
        run: node engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs
      - name: Conformance sweep (work scope)
        # The CHANGE, not the tree: this branch's diff against the base branch, the
        # only scope that can see what a commit did rather than what the repo now
        # holds. It used to run at the session's Stop hook and nowhere else, so a
        # rule about the change was enforced only where a session happened to be.
        #
        # The recipe — fetch the base, skip the engine's own branches, refuse an
        # empty scope, sweep — lives in the engine entry point, which every member
        # vendors and runs by the same one line. This repo is the one that runs it
        # from the repo root instead of the mount.
        #
        # --branch explicitly: the checkout above is a detached head at the PR's real
        # head sha, where `rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD` says "HEAD" and no branch name
        # is discoverable — so the skip for engine-authored branches would never fire.
        run: node engine/checks/ci-work-scope.mjs --branch "${{ github.head_ref || github.ref_name }}"
      - name: Growth write-surface gate
