input.body:
Closes #1100.

Versions were a plain monotonic counter. It orders releases, which is all the update flows need, but it says nothing about *when* one was cut: a member stamped at `6` against a canon at `13` is behind by an unknown amount of time, and every fleet surface reporting that gap makes a reader go and date it by hand.

Both the engine and every pack now version as `<day>.<n>` — `60820.1`, where the day part is `(year - 2020) * 10000 + month * 100 + day` and the second part is the running number of versions cut that day. Displayed with a leading `v`, as the surfaces already do.

Two decisions worth naming:

- **The year is anchored on 2020, not taken as its last digit.** A last-digit year wraps to `0` in 2030 and sorts a decade of releases underneath every 2029 one. `2026 → 6` either way, so the example holds and the ordering survives.
- **A version is a string.** `60820.10` and `60820.1` are different versions and the same float, so nothing in the corpus may parse one as a number.

### The migration technique

Every reader accepts **both** spellings. A legacy integer parses as `<n>.0`, which sorts below every date-anchored version — exactly where a member that has not re-stamped belongs, so no fleet surface has to special-case it. The tolerance is scheduled for removal in its own change, #1106, once the fleet has converged; the parser's own comment carries that date and issue number.

Legacy integers deliberately stay in two places for now: each pack's `minEngineVersion` floor and every migration record's `version:` range, both of which are references to engine versions that really were plain counters. #1106 retires them.

Zero stays readable and is *not* a legacy version — it is the install floor (DESIGN §3), so `isVersion(0)` is true while `isDeclaredVersion(0)` is false, and a stamp at the floor still reads as "says something" rather than as absence.

### What changed, by folder

- **`engine/`** — `version.mjs` gains the format: `parseVersion`, `compareVersions`, `versionsEqual`, `nextVersion`, `versionDay`, and `VERSION_SOURCE`, the regex fragment the text scrapers share so the six of them cannot disagree about what a version looks like. The helpers live beside the constant rather than in a module of their own, so the engine surface a mount must carry for any of it is one file. `ENGINE_VERSION` becomes `'60820.1'`. `pack_loader/pack-schema.mjs` validates both spellings, and `checks/helpers/active-migrations.mjs` reads a record's range and ranges over it through the shared comparator.
- **`updates/`** — the three planners (`engine-update`, `pack-update`, `install`) compare through `versionAbove` instead of `>` and gate on `isVersion` instead of `typeof === 'number'`.
- **`packs/`** — all 33 manifests move to `'60820.1'`. The dashboard's `fleet.mjs` and the sheepdog's `fleet-roster/drift-issues.mjs` scrape and compare through the shared helpers.
- **`.claudinite/local/packs/`** — `pack-version-bumped` and `engine-release-record`, the two canon-side checks that read a version out of a diff, do the same; the first now names `nextVersion(base)` as the remedy rather than `base + 1`.
- **`vendoring/rehearsal/fixtures.mjs`** — the `versioned-local` shape gains a second local pack carrying the date-anchored spelling. This is the `consumer-safe-change` answer: the manifest vocabulary widened, additively, and the fixture is what proves a consumer-authored manifest still validates in **both** spellings.

`ENGINE_VERSION` moving is an engine release, so it lands with its `RELEASES.md` row citing canary rehearsal [run 32371130795](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/32371130795), dispatched against this branch at `1f05d43`.

### One unrelated commit, and why it is here

The second commit fixes `a long work step leaves heartbeats on its own item`, which slept a fixed 40ms against a 5ms beat interval and asserted two beats had arrived. It is red on `origin/main` — three full-suite runs out of four at eight workers — and it was red on this branch's CI twice in a row, so nothing was going to make this PR green without it. The step now polls its own item until the second beat lands, under a 5s ceiling so a heartbeat that never fires stays a failed assertion rather than a hang. It is a separate commit and nothing else in the diff touches the scheduler.

### On delivery

This changes a contract member files carry (the stamp) and the engine flow that reads it, so "will it work on every repo?" is a live question rather than a uniform-by-construction change. Driving Shepherd's `fleet-baseline` with `follow`, and reporting per member, belongs to whoever merges this.

---

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files and comment-only changes.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files and comment-only changes.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

1	// THE ENGINE VERSION — the value that says which engine release a repo is running
2	// (docs/versioned-updates/DESIGN.md §2). The engine root vendors wholesale, so this
3	// module ships into every mount with the rest of the engine, and a member's stamp
4	// records the value it received (vendoring/apply-vendor-set.mjs). That pair is what
5	// makes "installed version → target version" answerable on the member side: which
6	// engine migrations still apply, and whether a pack's minimum is satisfied.
7	//
8	// DATE-ANCHORED, `<day>.<n>` — the shape, the ordering and why the corpus versions
9	// this way rather than in semver are stated below the constant. Every comparison made
10	// of this value is "installed < target" over a total order, so the format buys one
11	// thing over the plain counter it replaced: the version says when it was cut, without
12	// a second lookup.
13	//
14	// ADVANCED BY RELEASE, never by an ordinary change: a release is a snapshot that has
15	// passed the live canary rehearsal once (DESIGN §2.1), and the bump is what declares
16	// that happened. An engine migration is written against the version it lands in — it
17	// applies to repos below that value.
18	export const ENGINE_VERSION = '60820.1';
19	
20	// THE VERSION FORMAT — how every engine and pack version in the corpus is written,
21	// read and ordered. The helpers below are imported by every side that creates a
22	// version (each `packs/*/pack.mjs`), stamps one (updates/), compares two (the update
23	// planners, the dashboard, the fleet roster) or scrapes one out of source text over
24	// the API. They live beside the constant rather than in a module of their own so the
25	// engine surface a member's mount must carry for any of it is one file.
26	//
27	// THE SHAPE IS `<day>.<n>` — `60820.1`, displayed with a leading `v`. The day part
28	// is `(year - 2020) * 10000 + month * 100 + day`, so 2026-08-20 is 60820; the second
29	// part is the running number of versions cut on that day, starting at 1. It is a
30	// STRING and never a float: `60820.10` and `60820.1` are different versions and the
31	// same number.
32	//
33	// Anchoring the year on 2020 rather than taking its last digit is what keeps the day
34	// part monotonic past 2029 — 2030 reads 100101, above every 2029 value, where a
35	// last-digit year would wrap to 0 and sort a decade of releases underneath.
36	//
37	// WHY DATE-ANCHORED AT ALL. Every comparison the update flows make is still
38	// "installed < target" over a total order — nothing here needs semver's three
39	// components. What the plain counter could not do is say WHEN: a member stamped at 6
40	// against a canon at 13 is behind by an unknown amount of time, and the fleet
41	// surfaces that as a number a reader has to go and date by hand.
42	//
43	// LEGACY TOLERANCE, until 2026-08-27 (#1106). Versions were plain positive integers
44	// until 2026-08-20, and the integers are still sitting in every member's stamp, in
45	// each pack's `minEngineVersion` floor and in every migration record's range. So a
46	// legacy integer parses here as `<n>.0` — below every date-anchored version, which
47	// is exactly where a member that has not re-stamped belongs. Dependency-free, like
48	// the manifest spec it serves.
49	
50	// The day part of a Date, in UTC. Callers that have a `YYYY-MM-DD` string already
51	// (the corpus passes `today` around in that form) can hand it straight over.
52	export function versionDay(when = new Date()) {
53	  const d = typeof when === 'string' ? new Date(`${when.slice(0, 10)}T00:00:00Z`) : when;
54	  if (Number.isNaN(d.getTime())) return null;
55	  return (d.getUTCFullYear() - 2020) * 10000 + (d.getUTCMonth() + 1) * 100 + d.getUTCDate();
56	}
57	
58	// A date-anchored version, as its two parts. The day part is at least five digits
59	// (2020-01-01 is 101, but nothing predates the scheme, and the smallest day a repo
60	// can carry is 60820), which is what keeps it unambiguously apart from a legacy
61	// counter — those never reached three figures.
62	const DATE_ANCHORED = /^([1-9]\d{4,5})\.([1-9]\d*)$/;
63	
64	// A version in EITHER form, as `{ day, seq }`, or null when the value is not one.
65	// A legacy integer is `{ day: n, seq: 0 }` — the same tuple shape, so every
66	// comparison below is written once and knows nothing about the two spellings.
67	//
68	// ZERO IS READABLE and is not an absence: an install runs from version zero
69	// (docs/versioned-updates/DESIGN.md §3), so a stamp may hold one and it must sort
70	// below everything rather than read as "this stamp says nothing". Nothing may
71	// DECLARE it — that is `isDeclaredVersion` below.
72	export function parseVersion(v) {
73	  if (typeof v === 'number') return Number.isInteger(v) && v >= 0 ? { day: v, seq: 0 } : null;
74	  if (typeof v !== 'string') return null;
75	  const m = DATE_ANCHORED.exec(v.trim());
76	  return m ? { day: Number(m[1]), seq: Number(m[2]) } : null;
77	}
78	
79	export const isVersion = (v) => parseVersion(v) !== null;
80	
81	// What a manifest or a release may WRITE: a real version, never the install floor.
82	export const isDeclaredVersion = (v) => isVersion(v) && v !== 0;
83	
84	// True for the retiring spelling only — the one thing the removal change (#1106)
85	// greps for, and what a reader needing to say "this predates the scheme" asks.
86	export const isLegacyVersion = (v) => typeof v === 'number' && Number.isInteger(v) && v >= 0;
87	
88	// Order two versions: negative when `a` is older. An UNPARSEABLE version is not an
89	// error and not a zero — it sorts as equal to everything, so a caller that cannot
90	// price one side reports "no gap" rather than inventing one in either direction.
91	// Callers that must distinguish absence from equality check `isVersion` first.
92	export function compareVersions(a, b) {
93	  const x = parseVersion(a);
94	  const y = parseVersion(b);
95	  if (!x || !y) return 0;
96	  return x.day - y.day || x.seq - y.seq;
97	}
98	
99	export const versionAbove = (a, b) => compareVersions(a, b) > 0;
100	
101	// Equality has to ask more than `compareVersions(a, b) === 0`: an unpriceable side
102	// compares equal to everything, so the two versions must both be real ones first.
103	export const versionsEqual = (a, b) => isVersion(a) && isVersion(b) && compareVersions(a, b) === 0;
104	
105	export const formatVersion = ({ day, seq }) => `${day}.${seq}`;
106	
107	// The next version to cut today, given the one that stands. A new day restarts the
108	// running number at 1; a second version on the same day is `.2`. A `current` that is
109	// legacy, absent or unparseable simply does not constrain today's number — the day
110	// part is already above every integer the old scheme ever reached.
111	export function nextVersion(current, today = new Date()) {
112	  const day = versionDay(today);
113	  const held = parseVersion(current);
114	  return held && held.day === day ? `${day}.${held.seq + 1}` : `${day}.1`;
115	}
116	
117	// The version-shaped fragment for the text scrapers — the readers that lift a
118	// version out of `engine/version.mjs` or a `pack.mjs` fetched over the API, where
119	// there is nothing to import. Kept here so the six of them cannot disagree about
120	// what a version looks like; each wraps it in its own anchor.
121	export const VERSION_SOURCE = String.raw`\d+(?:\.\d+)?`;
122	
123	// What such a scraper should hand back: the literal as it was written, so a legacy
124	// integer stays a number and a date-anchored version stays a string, and every
125	// comparison downstream is the same one function.
126	export function versionFromLiteral(text) {
127	  if (text == null) return null;
128	  const t = String(text).trim();
129	  const v = t.includes('.') ? t : Number(t);
130	  return isVersion(v) ? v : null;
131	}

**2. Review and authorization gates — collapsed into one pass.** Every phase that ships code is a
gate: the owner must read it and approve it before the next phase can start. A plan with four
coding phases has four such waits, and each one is dead time whose length nobody controls.

Write **all** the code first, as a stack of PRs each based on the previous, and put the whole
stack in front of the owner together. The stack keeps the reviewable units small and independent —
one concern per PR, as ever — while costing one arrival of attention rather than four. Merge it
base-first once approved.

Approval of the stack is approval of the stack: it does not extend to a fix authored afterwards
(basics' *Acting on an approval to merge, ship or proceed*).

**3. Execution steps — whatever is left.** Once phase zero has landed the setup and the stack has
merged, the remaining steps run the migration: force the converge, backfill the members, watch the
cutover, retire the shim. If the first two sorts were done properly there is no gate among them —
they can be run at will, in one sitting, by whoever is at the keyboard.

That is the test of the plan. **Read the phases in order and mark every point where the run would
have to stop and wait for a person.** Each mark that falls after phase zero and the review pass is
a step that was sorted wrong. Move it, or say in the plan why it genuinely cannot move.

## The compatibility window, and why it is not a phase

A migration that changes a *representation* — a version format, a field's shape, a wire word, a
file layout — has a shortcut past most of the sort above, and it is worth reaching for
deliberately. Land it as **one change in which every reader takes both spellings and every writer
produces only the new one.** The old data keeps working where it stands, the new data is correct
from the first commit, and there is no cutover to schedule because there is no moment when
something must be true of everything at once.

What that leaves is a tail: the tolerance, which is dead weight and a second code path nobody will
remember is there. Do **not** write it into the plan as a later phase. A "remove the shim" phase is
the archetype of the phase that never closes — it has no owner at the moment it becomes due, the
run that would have done it ended weeks earlier, and nothing brings it back. File it instead as
work that comes back on its own (basics' *Spotting a change that should wait*), in the **same
change that opens the window**, and write into it:

- **The date or condition the window closes on**, and the observable that settles it — not "once
  everyone has migrated" but "no member's stamp still holds the old form", read from the thing that
  already reads it.
- **The full removal list.** The run that does it will not have this conversation: name every
  reader that took both, and every place the old spelling still legitimately stands.
- **What must survive the removal.** A tolerance usually sits next to something that looks
  identical and is not — a real zero beside an absent value, a legacy spelling beside a reserved
  one — and the removal run needs telling which is which.

Then **carry the expiry at the site**: the reader that accepts both says, where it does so, when
that stops and which issue removes it. The comment and the queued issue are one fact in two places,
and the one a future reader hits first is the code.

The same shape answers finding 3 below. A destructive step you can defer into a dual-read window
does not need to be scheduled against the cutover at all — it needs the window, and the issue that
closes it.

content.content:
---
name: merge-to-main
description: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
---

# Merge to main

If the project's own `CLAUDE.md` names a merge-policy file, that file overrides the divergent
points below (merge method, CI gating). Don't go hunting for one it doesn't name.

1. Load `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request` in one `ToolSearch`.
2. No PR open for the branch? `create_pull_request` (base `main`), body ending `Closes #<issue>`.
3. If the PR has check runs, wait for them to pass. None — merge without waiting.
4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Don't pre-read
   mergeability; the call fails loudly.
5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.
6. Capture the conversation:
   `node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`
   (in the canon repo: `node packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`). Skip only if
   the repo doesn't declare `claudinite-growth`. A later merge in the same session runs it again.
7. Run the basics pack's
   [verify-in-production](../../../basics/skills/verify-in-production/SKILL.md) skill, unasked.
   It decides whether this change needs a production check at all — most don't — and files the
   issue that comes back once the change is live. Never offer the owner to check later instead.

Don't re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge.

input.body:
Stacked on #1105 — it edits `packs/basics/`, whose version #1105 already moves, so this one bases on that branch and bumps to `60820.2`. Merge #1105 first; this retargets to `main` on its own.

The technique #1105 used is worth writing down, and the skill that should carry it is the one about ordering a plan's phases: **a migration's cleanup is filed as work that comes back on its own, never written as a later phase.** A cleanup phase falls due long after the run that would have done it ended, and nothing brings it back; filed as a queued issue in the same change that creates the thing it cleans up, the owner can forget about it, which is the point.

It goes in the destructive-step exception in §1 — the paragraph that already names the migration's tail — plus a clause on finding 3 in the review list. Five lines net.

*(First draft was a 38-line section with its own heading. The owner's read on it — "very verbose for [one sentence]" — was right, and the section is gone.)*

### What changed, by folder

- **`packs/basics/skills/writing-migration-plans/`** — the rule, in §1's exception and finding 3.
- **`packs/basics/`** — the manifest version, since a pack's content is delivered on it.
